title: When Would You NOT Use Microservices for This?
summary: Tests whether you can argue against the trendy default and name concrete costs — operational overhead, network hops, distributed debugging — microservices impose on a small team or simple domain.

slides.markdown:
The interviewer asks: **"when would you NOT use microservices for this?"** It's testing whether you can argue against "microservices are just best practice" — the assumption that decomposing into services is inherently more mature or correct.

A strong answer names concrete costs microservices impose (operational overhead, network hops, distributed debugging) and states plainly when a monolith is actually the better engineering call.

Ask about team size and how tightly coupled the actual business capabilities are. Does the domain have clean, stable seams — or would a service split cut through something that changes together constantly?

A domain that's still being redefined week to week doesn't have stable seams yet, no matter how cleanly it might eventually decompose. Splitting too early means renegotiating service boundaries as often as you'd otherwise renegotiate a single codebase's internal structure — but now across a network.

A monolith wins when the team is small, the domain isn't clearly separable yet, or low-latency in-process calls matter more than independent deployability.

Each of those three is independently sufficient — a small team can lack the separability problem entirely and still be better off monolithic simply because it doesn't need independent deploys badly enough to pay the network-hop cost.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: a 5-person startup's modular monolith
slides.markdown:
A 5-person startup chooses a modular monolith over microservices: one deployable, one on-call rotation, in-process function calls instead of network hops between "services" that would otherwise be owned by the same two engineers anyway.

Splitting here buys independent deployability the team doesn't need — there's no second team to deploy independently from — while paying real costs: more infrastructure to run, more places for a request to fail.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: a domain model that's still changing weekly
slides.markdown:
That same startup, still pre-product-market-fit, redesigns its core domain model every few weeks as it learns what customers actually want. Splitting into microservices now would mean renegotiating service boundaries and API contracts on the same weekly cadence — far more expensive across service boundaries than inside one codebase.

Inside a monolith, a domain redesign is a refactor. Across microservices, the same redesign is a coordinated, versioned API change across every service the affected boundary touches.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: what a service boundary specifically costs
slides.markdown:
![An in-process function call versus the same call across a service boundary, with added latency and failure mode](assets/call-boundary-cost.svg)

Every service boundary you add turns a function call into a network call — new latency, new failure mode. A single logical transaction that used to be one database transaction now needs a saga or eventual consistency across services.

This is the concrete, line-item cost behind the abstract phrase "distributed systems complexity" — it's specifically more latency and more ways for a single logical operation to partially fail.

slides.sectionTitle: The trade-off to name out loud
slides.markdown:
Microservices buy independent scaling and independent deployability at the direct cost of operational complexity (more moving parts to monitor, deploy, and debug) and distributed-systems failure modes a monolith never has to deal with.

That trade only pays off once you actually have the team scale or the scaling needs that justify it. Paying the cost before you have the need is pure downside — the independence you bought sits unused while the complexity is fully live.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: the team is now 50 people
slides.markdown:
Follow-up: "the team is now 50 people — has the calculus changed?" Likely yes. At that scale a monolith becomes a deployment and ownership bottleneck — everyone blocked on the same release train, unclear ownership of shared code — that microservices' independent deployability directly solves.

The answer isn't "microservices are now better in general," it's that the specific cost the monolith was avoiding (network hops, operational overhead) is now smaller than the specific cost it's now incurring (a shared release train blocking 50 engineers).

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: getting some benefits without the full cost
slides.markdown:
Follow-up: "can you get some of microservices' benefits without paying the full network-hop cost?" A modular monolith with strict internal module boundaries — enforced via code structure, not network calls — captures a lot of the organizational-clarity benefit while keeping calls in-process, as a middle ground.

This is worth naming because it shows the choice isn't binary: you can get clean ownership boundaries today and split the modules into real services later, once the network-hop cost is actually worth paying.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: adopting microservices because big companies do
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** adopting microservices for a small team because "that's what big companies do," without the team scale or domain separability that made it the right call for those companies.

**Why it's wrong:** the big companies you're copying adopted microservices to solve a specific problem — a shared release train blocking hundreds of engineers, or clean ownership boundaries between large, established teams — that a small team doesn't have yet.

**Correct model:** match the architecture to your own team's actual scale and domain stability, not to what a company solving a different problem chose.

A monolith wins when the team is small, the domain isn't yet separable, or in-process latency matters more than independent deployability. Name the concrete costs microservices impose — network hops replacing function calls, sagas replacing transactions, more operational surface area — rather than a vague "distributed systems are hard."

Be ready to flip the answer at real scale (a 50-person team hitting a shared release-train bottleneck) and to name the modular monolith as a middle ground. See [monolith-vs-microservices](monolith-vs-microservices) for the deeper technical trade-offs behind this call.
